summary.text: Archaea are a domain of life whose cells differ from bacteria and eukaryotes, with ether-linked lipid membranes and a unique motility structure called an archaellum.
The first ones observed lived in hot springs and salt lakes, but they are now found in almost every habitat, including soil, oceans and marshlands.
They are part of the microbiota of all organisms, and in humans they matter in the gut, mouth and skin.

facts.label: Classified apart
facts.value: 1977, by Carl Woese and George Fox

facts.label: Reproduction
facts.value: Asexually, by binary fission, fragmentation or budding

facts.label: Odd shape
facts.value: Haloquadratum walsbyi has flat, square cells

facts.label: Parasites
facts.value: As of 2024, only one species is known parasitic

items.prompt: Early scientists named this group "ancient things". Why?

options.label: Fossils of them were found in the oldest known rocks
Its first members were methanogens, assumed to reflect Earth's early atmosphere
They were the only life found in boiling springs
They had been known to doctors since antiquity

items.explain: The first representatives were methanogens, and it was assumed their metabolism reflected Earth's primitive atmosphere and their antiquity.

items.prompt: A friend says archaea live only in boiling springs and brine lakes. What is the best correction?

options.label: They have been found in almost every habitat, from soil to the oceans
They live only in extreme places, but more of them than once thought
They live in non-extreme places only, never in extreme ones
They live only inside other organisms

items.explain: Although the first observed archaea lived in extreme places, improved molecular detection found them in almost every habitat.

items.prompt: Researchers find a new group in a water sample, but nobody can grow it in a dish. How can they still identify it?

options.label: By waiting until it clouds a clean flask
By checking whether it forms spores
By reading ribosomal genes copied from the sample with PCR
By matching its cell shape to a book of drawings

items.explain: Most archaea have not been isolated in a laboratory and are identified by gene sequences in environmental samples, detected by multiplying their ribosomal genes with PCR.

items.prompt: Archaea look like bacteria in size and shape. Which part of their machinery resembles that of eukaryotes?

options.label: Their peptidoglycan cell walls, built like those of bacteria
Their ability to form tough, long-lived endospores
Their sexual way of reproducing by cell fusion
The genes and enzymes used in transcription and translation

items.explain: Despite similar size and shape, archaea have genes and metabolic pathways closer to eukaryotes, notably enzymes for transcription and translation.

items.prompt: A cow's gut holds vast numbers of methane-making archaea. What do they do for the cow?

options.label: They help it digest food
They live on it as parasites, as nearly all archaea do
They supply it with oxygen
They guard it from infection

items.explain: Only one archaeon species is known to be parasitic, and gut methanogens in ruminants facilitate digestion.

items.prompt: Cyanobacteria both get energy from the sun and build their own food. How do archaea compare?

options.label: Every archaeon does both jobs at once, just like cyanobacteria
Some run on sunlight and others fix carbon, but no known species does both
None of them can do either one, so they depend on other microbes
Only the few parasitic species can do either of these jobs

items.explain: Halobacteria use sunlight and other archaea fix carbon, but unlike cyanobacteria no known archaeon does both.
